chapman_belfast.text: Chapbooks, love! Boats built, books bound. Take your time, but not too much.

rail_guard.text: Grand Central. Trains to every station on this island you've visited. Please mind the gap, the step, and the seagull on the bench.
Hop aboard. The Wildlore rail runs to any town you have visited on this island. Where to?

then.text: Cairnryan, is it? The Selkie sails when the tide's right and the tea's brewed. Mind the gulls. They're organised.

else.text: Ah, the Selkie's not sailing for you yet, love. Scotland's a long way to go with an unfinished to-do list.
Go and see Keeper Ruairí at the shipyard first. Past the cranes, the big shed with the sparks. He's friendly. Mostly to people who've just lost to him, but still.

then.text: Grand day for the museum. Nobody minds a wee shower when there's fudge inside.
You're early! The building looks like four ship's hulls at sunrise. Worth the alarm clock.

titanic_guide.text: Welcome to Titanic Belfast! Harland and Wolff built the ship here, and it sailed in 1912. The story's sad, but the building is a joy, and the gift shop has a very good fudge.
Did you know the Titanic had a sister ship, the Olympic, built right alongside her? The Olympic sailed for 24 years. Nobody tells you that, because it's a lovely story with no iceberg.

then.text: Autumn winds up the Lagan. The cranes creak like old knees. Mine too, to be fair.
Frost on the quays. Samson and Goliath look grand in it. I look like a frozen pea.
Can't see Samson or Goliath in this fog. Doesn't matter, I know fine well they're there.
Sun on the cranes! They go bright yellow, like two big daffodils with jobs.
Knocking-off time. Samson and Goliath are the last thing I see on the way home.

dock_worker.text: I look up at Samson and Goliath every day. Hundred metres of yellow steel. They're no longer needed to build ships, but they're loved. We would never take them down.
On a Friday, the whole city looks up at them and says, 'right, that's us'. It's a Belfast thing.

then.text: That's a fair shirt. Derry made them by the million, you know.
St Patrick's Day, busiest day of my year. Every fare wants to sing to me.
Halloween's a whole week of fireworks here. The dog's under the bed till November.
Christmas market's up at City Hall. Folk ask me to drive round it twice. Same price both times, love.
Hop in out of that rain, so. Belfast drizzle's not weather, it's a lifestyle.
Wind's blowing a hoolie off the Lough. Hold on to your hat, and your wee dog.
Late one, is it? The city's quiet now, but the stories don't stop for bedtime.

black_taxi.text: {greeting} City tour? I'll take you round all of it, the shipyard, the Cathedral Quarter, the lot, and I'll tell you every story twice, once with feeling.
Belfast's got a sense of humour like nobody else's. It's the only city I know where 'not bad' is a standing ovation.

then.text: Told you. One-man wet session. The bodhrán's in a bin bag and still keeping time.
Sun's out in Belfast! Quick, everybody outside before it changes its mind.

park_busker.text: {greeting} Fiddle, whistle, and a bodhrán on my knee. I'm a one-man session. If the rain comes, I'll be a one-man wet session.
'Craic' is the word for fun and gossip. If you've had good craic, you've had a good time. If you've had bad craic, you've been in a meeting.

then.text: The Lagan's hiding in the fog this morning. The seals know where it is, mind.
The Big Fish glows lovely at dusk. Like it's had a good day too.

bridge_walker.text: The Lagan used to be so muddy you'd never guess there was a river. Now it's full of life: seals, salmon, even a few brave kayakers.
There's a huge fish sculpture down by the Waterfront, covered in tiles telling the history of Belfast. It's been called the Big Fish for over twenty-five years. Nobody has come up with a better name.

gate_belfast_north.text: Road's closed. Works on the Antrim coast. Very serious works. We've a cone.
The Keeper at the shipyard has the say on this road, and he hasn't said it yet. Ask Ruairí. Past the cranes, the big shed. You can't miss the sparks.

belfast_night_nurse.text: Off to the Royal for the night shift. Flask of tea, wee bag of biscuits, sorted.
Belfast's quiet at this hour. You can hear the Lagan if you stand still long enough.
Mind yourself getting home now. And get some sleep, I'll be jealous.

belfast_astronomer.text: I'm away up Cave Hill with the telescope. Clear nights here are rare, so you grab them.
From up there, the city lights look like stars fell into the Lough.
There's Orion. Big lad with a belt. Every winter he turns up, regular as a bus.

arts_harper.text: {greeting} Wire-strung, this one, like the old harpers played, with the nails. Gut and nylon came later, and so did the manicures.
In July 1792 they gathered ten harpers here, the last of the old tradition, and a lad of nineteen called Bunting wrote down every tune he could catch. Without that week we would have lost the lot.
Denis Hempson was nearly a hundred and had played for Bonnie Prince Charlie. He thought the others were all playing it wrong. He was probably right.
